nodes.label: J. L. Granatstein
nodes.date_label: Canada’s War (1975) · Broken Promises: with J. M. Hitsman (1977) · The Ottawa Men (1982) · Who Killed Canadian History? (1998)
nodes.description: A Canadian historian whose research connects wartime government, defence policy and military command. In a 2019 written interview he identifies the domestic politics of war and high command as his central interests, distinguishing them from battlefield narrative alone. His argument about the loss of national history also generated a historiographical dispute: the account here attributes that argument to A. B. McKillop’s critical reading and preserves the limits of the unread 1998 book.

Collective field comparisons retain their endpoints.

nodes.label: Joan Sangster
nodes.date_label: Dreams of Equality (1989) · “Beyond Dichotomies” (1995) · “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History” (2000) · Through Feminist Eyes: collection and retrospective introduction (2011)
nodes.description: A Canadian historian who brings feminist questions to labour history and treats the relationship between women’s history, gender analysis and class as an argument to be worked through. Her 2000 essay examines feminist challenges to a labour narrative centred on men and asks how race, ethnicity and gender change class formation. In her 2011 retrospective she explains that the 1995–96 exchange opposed a hierarchy that treated gender history as necessarily superior to women’s history. The entry preserves the difference between this retrospective and the original interventions.

nodes.scope_note: Existing scoped primary readings and the author’s later introduction are reused honestly; no new reading of Dreams of Equality, Regulating Girls and Women or Girl Trouble is claimed. The existing jointly authored 1992 reply to Bliss remains a separate intervention and is not recast as a reply to Granatstein’s 1998 book. No generic mentor or affiliation arrows.

nodes.label: Peter Burke
nodes.date_label: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978) · The French Historical Revolution: The Annales School, 1929–89 (1990) · What is Cultural History? (2004)
nodes.description: A cultural historian of early modern Europe who also writes about historical methods and the history of knowledge. His selected historiographical essay resists describing cultural history as a simple sequence in which each approach displaces the last. In a 2022 interview, he explains how Popular Culture combined wide comparison with attention to regional variation and discusses how changing scale alters historical explanation. The interview also insists on multiple historical voices, connecting structures with individual experience rather than choosing one for every inquiry.

nodes.scope_note: Two bounded primary discussions support method claims; the selected books’ complete bodies are unread here. The original 1978 book and revised editions, original 2004 book and later edition, and conversation/issue dates remain distinct. No blanket influence or affiliation inferred.

nodes.label: Jacques Le Goff
nodes.date_label: “Temps de l’Église et temps du marchand” (1960) · La Civilisation de l’Occident médiéval (1964) · La Naissance du Purgatoire: French original (1981) · The Birth of Purgatory: Arthur Goldhammer translation (1984)
nodes.description: A medieval historian who connects representations, everyday conditions and social organization. Jean-Claude Schmitt’s account, reproduced in the EPHE institutional notice, describes his medieval synthesis as attentive to material vulnerability, gestures, towns and intellectual activity. His work on purgatory advances a historically specific account of an intermediate place in the afterlife; that chronology remains a thesis to assess. His essays on medieval temporalities also supplied an explicitly acknowledged resource for E. P. Thompson’s discussion of work discipline.

nodes.scope_note: The monographs and Le Goff’s 1960/1963 essays are not newly read. Schmitt’s interpretation is attributed; Thompson’s p. 56 provides direct named-use testimony. The original Purgatory publisher/contents qualification remains. French originals and Goldhammer’s translation are distinct; no career interval or exclusive Annales identity.

nodes.label: Philippe Ariès
nodes.date_label: Histoire des populations françaises et de leurs attitudes devant la vie (1948) · L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960) · Centuries of Childhood: Robert Baldick translation (1962) · L’Homme devant la mort (1977)
nodes.description: A historian of family, childhood and attitudes toward death whose work made familiar social arrangements appear historically variable. The childhood argument concerns the historical recognition of childhood; it is not equivalent to claiming that earlier parents never loved their children. Linda Pollock’s criticism questions evidential representativeness and generalization. Jean-Claude Chamboredon’s obituary places Ariès’s studies in dialogue with sociological questions about institutions and modernity, while explaining their politically and professionally unusual setting.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Histoire des populations françaises et de leurs attitudes devant la vie depuis le XVIIIe siècle (1948); L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960); Centuries of Childhood, translated by Robert Baldick (1962); L’Homme devant la mort (1977).
nodes.scope_note: Ariès’s complete books are unread here. Existing Pollock primary-excerpt qualifications are retained and Chamboredon is named as the substantive reader. No absence-of-parental-affection claim. French originals and Baldick’s translation remain distinct. The death-day discrepancy is kept in life research rather than resolved by assumption.

nodes.label: Linda Colley
nodes.date_label: Britons: Forging the Nation (1992) · Captives (2002) · The Ordeal of Elizabeth Marsh: A Woman in World History (2007)
nodes.description: A historian of Britain, empire and global connections. Her selected works move from the making of British identity to captivity and an individual woman’s transcontinental life. In her 2016 written interview she explains how captivity narratives can expose imperial weakness as well as power, provided they are embedded in other research. She describes Elizabeth Marsh as a way of writing global history through a woman’s constrained and mobile life, reconstructing her through dispersed sources rather than treating biography as an isolated portrait.

No affiliation or mentor arrows, no universal account of Britishness, and no citation-count claim of influence.

nodes.label: Georges Duby
nodes.date_label: Le Dimanche de Bouvines (1973) · Les Trois Ordres ou l’Imaginaire du féodalisme (1978) · The Three Orders: Arthur Goldhammer translation (1980)
nodes.description: A medieval historian whose work connects economic and social arrangements with kinship, imagined orders and representations. Marc Verdure’s Collège de France account situates that method in relation to Bloch and Febvre while identifying distinct subjects rather than an exclusive school allegiance. Le Dimanche de Bouvines also became an example in Lawrence Stone’s narrative debate: the entry retains the difference between a historian’s chosen presentation and abandoning analysis. The Three Orders examines social classification; its imagined hierarchy is not a census of occupations.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Le Dimanche de Bouvines (1973); Les Trois Ordres ou l’Imaginaire du féodalisme (1978); The Three Orders: Feudal Society Imagined, translated by Arthur Goldhammer (1980); Histoire des femmes en Occident, co-directed with Michelle Perrot (1991–1992).
nodes.scope_note: Existing bounded readings by Verdure, Stone and Hobsbawm remain named and qualified. Duby’s complete books and original inaugural lecture are not newly read. Histoire des femmes remains co-directed with Michelle Perrot and 1991–1992; other contributors’ chapters are not reassigned. No blanket narrative turn, sole authorship or continuous career interval.

nodes.label: Gail Bederman
nodes.date_label: “The Women Have Had Charge of the Church Work Long Enough” (1989) · “‘Civilization,’ the Decline of Middle-Class Manliness…” (1992) · Manliness and Civilization: original publication (1995)
nodes.description: A historian of gender and race in the United States. Manliness and Civilization asks how changing ideals of manhood could reinforce white authority while also being contested. Its selected chapter opening distinguishes the projects of Wells, Hall, Gilman and Roosevelt rather than making them one coordinated movement. Anne-Marie Harvey’s substantive discussion identifies Bederman’s account of a shift from self-restraint toward celebrated masculine force; that account is retained as an interpretation with a later reader’s qualifications, not a universal sequence.

nodes.scope_note: New identity is the Notre Dame historian and sole author of the selected writings. Both early articles and full monograph unread. Argument evidence is limited to the indexed primary passage and Harvey’s explicitly attributed discussion; direct scan access failed. The primary extract preserves differences among the historical actors. No claim of a uniform white masculinity or a direct intellectual influence on later scholars.

nodes.label: Jackson Lears
nodes.date_label: No Place of Grace (1981) · Fables of Abundance (1994) · Something for Nothing: Luck in America (2003)
nodes.description: A cultural historian of the United States whose work connects religious longing, commercial persuasion and the making of meaning. In his written exchange with B. R. Cohen he explains cultural history as an inquiry into meanings formed through lived anxieties and desires, including unintended consequences. Advertising is examined through trust and confidence as well as sales. His conversation with David Serlin describes chance and control as intertwined practices rather than mutually exclusive eras, linking gambling, belief and economic life without claiming that calculation eliminates uncertainty.

nodes.label: Antoine Prost
nodes.date_label: Histoire de l’enseignement en France, 1800–1967 (1968) · Les Anciens Combattants et la société française: three-volume publication (1977) · Douze leçons sur l’histoire (1996)
nodes.description: A French historian of education, social life and the aftermath of war who also examines historical knowledge and practice. Maurice Agulhon’s substantive reading describes the veterans study as joining organization, social composition and commemorative practices, while challenging an automatic identification of veterans with fascism. Agulhon also questions whether that correction goes too far. Danièle Voldman reads Douze leçons as both a methodological exposition and a situated defence of historical understanding. These readings support the entry without claiming that the underlying books have been read in full.

nodes.scope_note: New identity is the French historian of education and veterans, distinguished from other Prost authors by matching institutional and publication records. Argument claims use named substantive readers Agulhon and Voldman. Book bodies remain unread. Billois’s collaboration, the three-volume format, original publication years and separate shorter/late editions stay explicit. No generic university, political-affiliation or influence arrows.

edges.relationship: Connects military history to the domestic politics of wartime government and the politics of high command.
edges.evidence_note: Author’s written answer to “Why did you choose to focus so much of your work on Canada’s role in the world wars?” (2019). This is his research emphasis, not an endorsement of every military or political judgment in the interview.

edges.relationship: Makes the disputed charge that specialization and ideological commitments have displaced national history.
edges.evidence_note: As characterized and challenged in A. B. McKillop’s 1999 abstract, already read in the graph. The polemic itself remains unread. This arrow identifies a contested intervention, not proof of its diagnosis or a general rejection of social history.

edges.relationship: Uses feminist critiques to reconsider gender, race and ethnicity within accounts of working-class formation.
edges.evidence_note: Reuse of the recorded abstract and bounded 2000 essay readings. The field’s masculinist starting points are Sangster’s diagnosis. This does not infer a single causal genealogy from political organizing.

edges.relationship: Questions treating women’s history and gender history as opposed stages in an inevitable methodological succession.
edges.evidence_note: The 2011 introduction’s own retrospect supports this formulation; existing addenda separately record full readings of the two original essays. The disagreement and Sangster’s concessions remain situated, not an assertion that all gender historians held one position.

edges.relationship: Questions a simple replacement model of cultural approaches while investigating historical meanings and cultural variation.
edges.evidence_note: Reuse of the existing essay reading, PDF pp. 1–13 and selected opening of p. 14. The arrow adopts its limited anti-succession argument, not all of Burke’s survey or a verified genealogy for every predecessor.

edges.relationship: Explains how changes in research scale alter plausible explanations, linking regional cultural variation with wider comparisons.
edges.evidence_note: Primary interview, question 7, read. Burke discusses the scale question and describes his own popular-culture research; this is a methodological contribution, not membership in one microhistorical school or a claim that he invented scale analysis.

edges.relationship: Relates medieval representations and everyday material conditions within a social history attentive to belief and vulnerability.
edges.evidence_note: Substantive characterization is attributed to Jean-Claude Schmitt’s account reproduced in the EPHE notice. The existing Purgatory publisher record is supplementary; it does not establish that the monograph was read or that its chronology is uncontested.

edges.relationship: Supplies a specifically acknowledged resource on merchant and ecclesiastical temporalities in Thompson’s 1967 time-discipline essay.
edges.evidence_note: Primary p. 56 and n. 2 checked afresh: Thompson explicitly identifies Le Goff’s contrast and cites the 1960 and 1963 essays. This records that limited use, not the whole derivation of Thompson’s argument or a universal account of modernization. Le Goff’s cited essays remain unread here.

edges.relationship: Makes the historical concept of childhood a problem for family history, while prompting disputes over sources and generalization.
edges.evidence_note: The formulation retains Pollock’s distinction between concept and affection and her source criticism (1983 excerpt pp. 1–10, especially 2 and 6–9). It neither endorses Ariès’s chronology nor reassigns later writers’ stronger claims to him.

edges.relationship: Historicizes familiar family institutions and social attitudes, opening comparative questions between modernity and earlier arrangements.
edges.evidence_note: Attributed to Jean-Claude Chamboredon, 1985 pp. 150–151, on the work’s sociological questions and the family/death studies. This is a named reader’s substantive assessment, not a claim that Ariès belonged to a single sociological school.

edges.relationship: Uses captivity accounts, contextualized with other research, to examine imperial vulnerability and uneven encounters.
edges.evidence_note: Author’s 2016 interview answers on the genesis and interpretation of Captives. This contribution concerns a research method and its selected object; her monograph has not been read in full.

edges.relationship: Uses Elizabeth Marsh’s itinerant life to investigate transcontinental connections and women’s place in global history.
edges.evidence_note: Author’s answers on biography, missing letters and reconstructing Marsh through others’ writings. This identifies a specific biographical project, without treating one life as representative of every woman or attributing the book’s sources to Colley.

edges.relationship: Relates medieval economic and social arrangements to imaginaries, kinship and marriage.
edges.evidence_note: Methodological characterization attributed to Marc Verdure’s institutional account of the 1970 inaugural lecture, not a fresh reading of that lecture. Existing Orders description/contents are supplementary; their suspect seventh-century wording is not used.

edges.relationship: Provides a case for debating the relation between narrative presentation and historical analysis through Le Dimanche de Bouvines.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive readers: Stone 1979, read pp. 3–6 and 13–24 only, and Hobsbawm’s complete 1980 response. Duby’s book itself remains unread. This records the use of his work in the debate, not his acceptance of Stone’s entire historiographical diagnosis.

edges.relationship: Treats ideals of manhood as historical constructions whose forms and political uses change.
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary indexed passage, pp. 42–43, plus Anne-Marie Harvey’s substantive reading at printed pp. 42–43. The latter names Bederman’s distinction and extends it in her own study; her additions are not reassigned to Bederman.

edges.relationship: Investigates how claims about civilization could authorize white male power or be turned against it.
edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter-1 closing passage on four distinct cases, indexed printed pp. 42–43. The prose on historical actors is Bederman’s argument, not an endorsement of their racial categories. No claim that the entire book or its cited archival evidence was independently read.

edges.relationship: Defines cultural history through historically situated meanings, conflicting desires and unintended consequences.
edges.evidence_note: Author answers in the Cohen interview, section II; Serlin interview answers on overlapping chance/control. These are Lears’s stated interpretive methods, not certification of each example or a field-wide consensus.

edges.relationship: Connects commercial persuasion to culturally specific practices of confidence, trust and uncertainty.
edges.evidence_note: Cohen interview, section I, where Lears discusses Fables of Abundance and the historical settings of confidence. The complete advertising monograph remains unread and no timeless national character is inferred.

edges.relationship: Integrates veterans’ organizations and commemorative practices into a social history of postwar France.
edges.evidence_note: Agulhon 1979, pp. 831–832, read: specifically discusses November 11 ceremonies, monuments and village sociability. His account of Prost’s political correction includes reservations about its extent. No uncritical consensus or whole-book reading.

edges.relationship: Makes methods, question formation and the historian’s social position explicit problems of historical knowledge.
edges.evidence_note: Voldman’s substantive 1996 review, pp. 174–175, attributes this methodological and epistemological argument to Douze leçons. The book itself remains unread; this is not an inferred connection from its title alone.
